extracted.intended_audience: USPTO-registered practitioners, their counsel, OED staff, and administrative law judges handling USPTO disciplinary matters
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive standards for prosecuting, defending, and deciding disciplinary proceedings against practitioners before the USPTO under 35 U.S.C. § 32 and 37 C.F.R. part 11, including discovery, sanctions, summary judgment, and burden of proof rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory/regulatory authority for discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO has the 'exclusive authority to establish qualifications for admitting persons to practice before it, and to suspend or exclude them from practicing before it.' This authority flows from 35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(D) (regulations governing conduct) and 35 U.S.C. § 32 (discipline). The Rules of Professional Conduct for USPTO practitioners are codified at 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.101 to 11.901, and disciplinary hearings follow 37 C.F.R. part 11 and 5 U.S.C. § 556.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these statutory and regulatory provisions as the controlling framework for jurisdiction, permissible charges, and procedure in USPTO disciplinary cases; cite them when asserting or challenging authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard and burden of proof in disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving any alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence, and the respondent bears the burden of proving any affirmative defenses by clear and convincing evidence. (37 C.F.R. § 11.49.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear and convincing is an intermediate standard between 'beyond a reasonable doubt' and 'preponderance'—requiring evidence that 'produces in the mind of the trier of fact a firm belief or conviction, without hesitancy' or that proves the facts to be 'highly probable.' Authorities (e.g., Jimenez v. DaimlerChrysler Corp.) may be cited to define the standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'clear and convincing' evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear and convincing evidence requires evidence of such weight that it 'produces in the mind of the trier of fact a firm belief or conviction, without hesitancy, as to the truth of the allegations sought to be established' or 'proves the facts at issue to be 'highly probable.''
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the sufficiency of proof, tribunals should apply this intermediate standard; parties should tailor presentation of documentary and testimonial proof to meet this heightened showing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural framework for hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary hearings are conducted in accordance with 37 C.F.R. part 11 and with section 7 of the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 556, by an impartial hearing officer appointed by USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure procedural compliance with part 11 (notice, opportunity to be heard, discovery rules, motions practice) and with APA adjudicative requirements; parties should prepare for formal evidentiary procedures similar to civil litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery authorization and scope (37 C.F.R. § 11.52)
rubrics_metrics.description: Written discovery is governed by 37 C.F.R. § 11.52. The regulation allows the tribunal to authorize interrogatories, requests for production, and requests for admission upon a motion demonstrating the reasonableness and relevance of each request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motions for discovery must show reasonableness and relevance of each request. Parties should draft narrowly tailored requests and be prepared to justify them in a motion; the Court may authorize discovery akin to Federal Rules practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to compel and application of Fed. R. Civ. P. 37
rubrics_metrics.description: If the party answering discovery fails to respond or provides an 'evasive and incomplete' response, the party seeking discovery may file a motion to compel; Fed. R. Civ. P. 37 (as applied by 37 C.F.R. § 11.43) guides available relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Federal Rules are not binding, they are helpful guidance for motions to compel and for framing sanctions; parties should cite Fed. R. Civ. P. 37 analogues when moving to compel or defending a motion to compel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions for discovery failures
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO regulations do not specifically provide sanctions for discovery failures, but under Fed. R. Civ. P. 37 a court may, among other things, 'direct that the matters embraced in the order or other designated facts be taken as established for purposes of the action' or 'prohibiting the disobedient party from supporting or opposing designated claims or defenses, or from introducing designated matters into evidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunals may employ exclusionary and deeming sanctions (e.g., deeming RFAs admitted, precluding evidence) modeled on Fed. R. Civ. P. 37; sanctions should be proportionate and justified by the discovery misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific sanctions applied for inadequate discovery responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Where respondent failed to provide complete and adequate responses to enumerated interrogatories, requests for production, and requests for admission, the Court precluded the respondent from offering testimony or documentary evidence that would have been responsive to those requests unless he could show prior production, and deemed specified requests for admission admitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions may be tailored: (1) preclusion of evidence responsive to unanswered requests, subject to showing prior production; (2) deeming requests for admission admitted; (3) other relief the Court deems just. Parties should promptly remedy deficiencies where ordered or face specific preclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet-and-confer requirement before filing motions (37 C.F.R. § 11.43)
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions must include a statement that, before filing, the movant conferred with opposing counsel in a good faith effort to resolve the issues and determine whether the motion is opposed, as required by 37 C.F.R. § 11.43.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to comply with the meet-and-confer requirement may result in summary denial or striking of the motion. Parties should document and include a good-faith confer statement (who was contacted, dates, results) with every motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for failing to comply with procedural filing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated failures to comply with basic filing requirements (e.g., § 11.43) can lead to warnings, striking of motions, and summary denial of future motions absent new law or facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondents should not file motions that ignore procedural prerequisites; courts expect compliance and may refuse to consider procedurally defective filings regardless of their substantive merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior state-court findings and collateral estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings rendered against a respondent in prior state-court judgments may be entitled to preclusive effect under the doctrine of collateral estoppel and can support partial summary judgment in USPTO proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunals may treat facts established in prior final judgments as preclusive if preclusion doctrine requirements are satisfied; parties should identify, authenticate, and brief preclusive effect of prior judgments when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for summary judgment in USPTO disciplinary cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The tribunal may grant summary judgment when no material facts remain in dispute; where 'the facts ... do not appear to be genuinely disputed' the Court may enter judgment as a matter of law on those facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking or opposing summary judgment, focus on whether genuine disputes of material fact exist; present admissible evidence and identify facts that should be deemed established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability and limits of laches defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Laches is unavailable in cases where a statute of limitations governs (e.g., 35 U.S.C. § 32); laches is predicated on inexcusable delay in instituting suit and cannot substitute for or override a statutory limitations period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on laches when the governing statute sets explicit time limits; instead, raise statute-of-limitations defenses with supporting factual and legal proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for requests to move deadlines or hearing dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests to move deadlines or hearing dates must be supported by documentation corroborating the need for the change (e.g., documentation establishing preexisting scheduling conflict or emergency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere assertions of unavailability are insufficient; submit objective corroborating documentation and comply with meet-and-confer requirements when seeking continuances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for reconsideration motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions seeking reconsideration of prior rulings should be supported by new law or facts; repetitive or spurious requests to revisit rulings absent new evidence or legal authority are disfavored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before filing reconsideration, establish a clear basis (newly discovered evidence, intervening controlling law, manifest error) and adhere to procedural requirements, or the motion risks summary denial or being stricken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverse inference from discovery non-production (discretionary)
rubrics_metrics.description: A court may draw an adverse inference that failure to timely correct deficient discovery responses indicates the withheld information would have supported the opposing party's claims, but such inferences are discretionary and may be declined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking adverse inferences, demonstrate the significance of the missing discovery and the respondent's culpability; be aware the tribunal may choose lesser sanctions (e.g., evidence preclusion, deeming RFAs) instead of an adverse inference on the merits.
